title: Complex Lp Spaces and Test-Function Conventions

items.title: Complex Lp classes and Euclidean test-function conventions
items.statement: For a measure space and 1 <= p <= infinity, a complex function is measurable when its real and imaginary parts are measurable. Define the modulus p-functional (extended value allowed), the finite-functional class, and its quotient by equality almost everywhere; p=infinity uses essential supremum of the modulus. Complex C_c, C_0, and C_c^infinity on R^n mean both components lie in the published real spaces; partial derivatives are componentwise. Finite simple functions have finite range; finite-measure support means mu({s != 0})<infinity, not compact topological support. Complex integration is the earlier component integral. The raw L2 pairing convention is integral f conjugate(g), linear in the first argument; bilinear tests use integral f s. These two pairings must not be conflated. For a topological space equipped with a measure on a sigma-algebra containing its Borel sets, define essential support as the complement of the union of open sets on which the function is zero almost everywhere; this is distinct from the closure of its nonzero set. On R^n with Lebesgue measure, locally integrable means measurable with integrable modulus on every compact subset; this is equivalent to integrability on every bounded ball. In the following Lebesgue illustration assume countable choice: the indicator of Q has essential supremum zero and empty essential support for Lebesgue measure, but ordinary support R; its essential supremum for the Dirac measure at zero is one.
items.strategy: Define the set quotient by a.e. equality before claiming it is a normed complex vector space. Measurability of modulus, products and conjugates follows by the real arithmetic closure and square-root composition; give the coordinate formulas. The first L2 formula is a convention on representatives whose integrability and class invariance are established below. For u=Re f and v=Im f, |f|=sqrt(u^2+v^2); for a>=0 its upper threshold is {u^2+v^2>a^2}, and for a<0 it is X. This proves the square-root step directly without a Euclidean Borel lemma carrying additional choice assumptions. The essential-support definition is class-independent since a change on one measurable null set preserves the zero-a.e. property on every open set. For local integrability, |Re f|,|Im f|<=|f|<=|Re f|+|Im f| proves componentwise equivalence; Euclidean compact sets are bounded and closed balls are compact, proving the ball equivalence. For the indicator illustration, use the earlier countable-null-set proposition with its countable-choice hypothesis, density of Q for ordinary support, and delta_0({0})=1 for the Dirac essential bound.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis
references.locator: §10.1, pp.281–283, formulas (10.1)–(10.7); §10.4, pp.294–298. Pairing convention cross-checked against Laugesen Ch.1, pp.9–10. Teschl (10.5), p.282, conjugates the first variable; this scaffold reverses that convention as required by MT-16c.

items.title: Complex Holder, Minkowski, and the quotient norm
items.statement: On every measure space, for conjugate exponents p,p′ in [1,infinity], complex f in Lp and g in Lp′ satisfy integral |fg| <= ||f||p ||g||p′ and |integral fg| <= ||f||p ||g||p′. For each 1 <= p <= infinity, ||f+g||p <= ||f||p+||g||p. Complex vector operations and the modulus norm are independent of representatives and define a norm on the a.e. quotient. Conjugation preserves the norm; both component norms are <= ||f||p <= ||Re f||p+||Im f||p.
items.strategy: Apply published real Holder to |f|,|g| and the integral triangle inequality. Use |f+g| <= |f|+|g| and real Minkowski, including the essential-bound endpoint. Zero norm iff zero a.e., scalar homogeneity, and union of finitely many measurable null sets prove the quotient assertions. The component comparison is pointwise then monotonicity; no abstract Banach space theorem.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis

items.title: Complex Lp completeness and almost-everywhere subsequences
items.statement: Assume countable choice. On an arbitrary measure space, complex Lp is complete for every 1 <= p <= infinity. Every norm-convergent sequence has a subsequence of measurable representatives converging a.e. to a representative of its norm limit. No assertion that the whole sequence converges pointwise is made for finite p.
items.strategy: Real and imaginary part maps are well-defined contractions on classes by the preceding theorem. Apply real Riesz–Fischer separately to the two component Cauchy sequences and recombine their limits using the component upper bound. For a.e. convergence extract first a real-part subsequence and then an imaginary-part subsequence of that subsequence; the union of their exceptional measurable null sets is null. Countable choice covers simultaneous representatives and approximation choices; set the representative to zero on exceptional sets to preserve measurability even for incomplete measures.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis

items.title: Complex finite-simple and smooth compact-support density for finite p
items.statement: For arbitrary measure spaces and 1 <= p < infinity, complex finite simple functions with finite-measure support are dense in Lp. Assuming countable choice, C_c^infinity(R^n;C) is dense in Euclidean Lebesgue Lp for the same finite exponents; hence C_c is dense too. These density assertions do not assert density of finite-support tests or smooth functions in all of Linfinity. The uniform closure of complex C_c in Linfinity(R^n) consists of classes with a C_0 representative.
items.strategy: Approximate each component using the earlier real finite-simple theorem; refine their finite partitions and unite their finite-measure nonzero sets. Sum the two norm errors by H. For smooth density use the real smooth-density theorem twice; the union of two compact supports is compact. For the final endpoint description use the real C_0 closure theorem on both components, including its identification of the supremum and essential-supremum norms for continuous functions. Do not use false global density of finite-measure-supported tests in Linfinity.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis
references.locator: Problem 10.17, p.293; Theorems 10.16 and 10.20, pp.294 and 298; endpoint paragraph after 10.16.

items.title: The complex L2 pairing on equivalence classes
items.statement: For f,g in complex L2(mu), propose <f,g> = integral f conjugate(g) dmu, computed from representatives. This is the first-variable-linear convention; its class invariance and inner-product axioms are the obligation of the following theorem.
items.strategy: Holder makes the representative product integrable. Keep the well-definedness theorem after this raw definition and name it only in justified_by.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis
references.locator: §10.2, Theorem 10.4 (p=2); convention: Laugesen Ch.1, p.10. Teschl (10.5), p.282, conjugates the first variable; this scaffold reverses that convention as required by MT-16c.

items.title: The complex L2 pairing is well-defined and satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz
items.statement: On every measure space the proposed L2 pairing is representative-independent, linear in the first variable, conjugate-linear in the second, conjugate symmetric, and positive definite on a.e. classes, with <f,f>=||f||2^2. It obeys |<f,g>| <= ||f||2 ||g||2. For nonzero g, equality holds exactly when f=cg a.e. for some c in C; if g=0 equality holds for every f. For any finite tuple of L2 functions the sum of these pairings is an inner product, with norm squared equal to the sum of the squared component norms; the same Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and common-scalar equality criterion hold for tuples.
items.strategy: Use complex integral linearity and its component definition to commute conjugation with integration, and use a.e.-invariance for the product. Positive definiteness is the zero nonnegative integral theorem. For g!=0 set c=<f,g>/||g||2^2 and expand ||f-cg||2^2=||f||2^2-|<f,g>|^2/||g||2^2. Nonnegativity gives the inequality; vanishing is equivalent to equality and to f=cg as classes. This proves the axioms directly without a later abstract inner-product theorem. Apply the identical nonnegative quadratic expansion to the finite sum for the tuple extension; a sum of nonnegative component norms vanishes exactly when every component vanishes. This retains the finite-tuple use mentioned in the historical stable interface.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis
references.locator: §10.2, Theorem 10.4 and p=2 discussion, pp.285–286; equality proof is the local quadratic expansion. Teschl (10.5), p.282, conjugates the first variable; this scaffold reverses that convention as required by MT-16c.

items.title: Complex completeness, density, and inner product: the consumer interface
items.statement: Assume countable choice. Complex Lp is complete for 1 <= p <= infinity, has a.e.-convergent subsequences of norm-convergent sequences, and for finite p has finite-simple density and Euclidean smooth compact-support density. Complex L2 carries the first-variable-linear pairing of the preceding definition with norm ||.||2 and the stated Cauchy–Schwarz equality criterion.
items.strategy: Collect the separately proved completeness, density, and pairing theorems. Preserve this staged stable lemma ID for its Fourier consumers; do not hide new proof obligations in an omnibus assertion.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis
references.locator: §10.3, 10.12–10.13; §10.4, 10.20; §10.2, p=2. Teschl (10.5), p.282, conjugates the first variable; this scaffold reverses that convention as required by MT-16c.

items.title: Complex Lq norm recovery from finite simple dual tests
items.statement: Let Sigma_fin be the complex finite simple functions whose nonzero sets have finite measure, and let q′ be conjugate to q in [1,infinity]. On a sigma-finite measure space, if g is complex measurable and g s is integrable for every s in Sigma_fin, then ||g||q = sup{|integral g s| : s in Sigma_fin, ||s||q′ <= 1}, with extended values allowed. In particular a finite uniform bound on these tests proves membership in Lq and gives its norm. If g is already in Lq, the same identity holds on arbitrary measure spaces for q<infinity, and on semifinite measure spaces for q=infinity. The pairing is bilinear; a sesquilinear formulation conjugates the test. The zero test is allowed, so the formula includes zero measure spaces.
items.strategy: Prove measurability of theta(g)=conjugate(g)/|g| off {g=0}, zero on it, by coordinate formulas. On a finite-measure set where g is bounded, write g_E=g 1_E and, when ||g_E||q>0, use h=1_E theta(g)|g|^(q-1)/||g_E||q^(q-1) for 1<q<infinity, h=theta(g) for q=1, and an L1-normalized phase on a positive almost-maximal level set for q=infinity. Approximate h uniformly on this finite set by finite-valued complex functions and divide by max(1,||s||q′); uniform error controls integral g(s-h) since g is integrable there. For q=1 use a finite grid in the closed unit disk, not norm density of finite-support functions in Linfinity. Exhaust sigma-finite X by E_n intersect {1/n<=|g|<=n}; monotone convergence recovers finite-q norms and level-set exhaustion recovers essential supremum, even if infinite. For g already in Lq with q finite, its positive level sets have finite measure so the same truncation works without sigma-finiteness. For bounded g at q=infinity, semifiniteness gives the finite positive almost-maximal test set. The one-point measure of infinite mass demonstrates why that hypothesis cannot simply be erased. Reciprocal and nonnegative real powers are measurable by their explicit threshold preimages; multiply by the measurable indicator of {g!=0} for the phase. Skip zero-norm truncations. Choose the exhaustion increasing (replace its sets by finite unions). A uniform simple approximation on a finite set also converges in every finite exponent norm, so normalization preserves convergence to each unit-norm extremizer.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis
references.locator: §10.2, Corollary 10.5 and Lemma 10.6, pp.286–287. Independent endpoint warning: Laugesen Appendix C, p.172.

items.title: Complex translation, convolution, approximate identities, and mollification
items.statement: Assume countable choice. On complex Euclidean Lebesgue Lp, translation tau_h f(x)=f(x-h) is an isometry for 1<=p<=infinity and norm-continuous in h for p<infinity. For K in complex L1 and f in complex Lp, K*f exists a.e., is class-independent, and ||K*f||p<=||K||1||f||p. If integral K_epsilon=1, sup ||K_epsilon||1<infinity, and integral_{|y|>=delta}|K_epsilon(y)| tends to zero for every delta>0, then K_epsilon*f tends to f in Lp for p<infinity, and uniformly for f in complex C_0. Kernels may be complex or sign-changing. For a real unit-mass smooth compactly supported mollifier rho_epsilon and complex locally integrable f, convolution is smooth and partial^alpha(rho_epsilon*f)=(partial^alpha rho_epsilon)*f; compactly supported inputs yield compact support. No general Linfinity norm-continuity or approximation assertion is allowed.
items.strategy: Translation and smoothness reduce to real and imaginary parts using the published real interfaces. Define complex convolution through its four real convolutions using Borel representatives; absolute convergence and the sharp norm estimate follow from |K*f|<=|K|*|f| and real Young. For the error apply integral triangle and real Minkowski-integral to the nonnegative envelope |K_epsilon(y)| |f(x-y)-f(x)|. This gives the exact small-translation/tail bound without assuming real and imaginary parts of a complex kernel are separately mass-one approximate identities. Treat the uniform C_0 conclusion directly by uniform continuity and the same split. The derivative and support assertions use the real mollifier and compact-support theorems componentwise. Extend representative independence directly to L1*Lp: if the two representatives change on null sets N_K,N_f, then for each fixed x the y-integrands agree off N_K union (x-N_f), a measurable null set by translation and reflection invariance. At points of absolute convergence their integrals agree by integral a.e.-invariance. The earlier L1*L1 representative lemma alone is not a supplier for this generalization. For each fixed compact x-neighbourhood, every kernel derivative has y-support in one compact set K and is bounded there by a constant C_alpha. The integrable majorant C_alpha |f| 1_K gives continuity of each derivative integral by dominated convergence, as well as the differentiation formula; existence of all partial derivatives alone is not used to infer continuity. For bounded continuous C_0 input the convolution is continuous by uniform continuity and the L1 bound, and vanishes at infinity by dominated convergence. The Borel representatives are obtained componentwise from the base-measurable-representative theorem, setting infinite values to zero on their Borel null sets.

title: Complex Lp Spaces and Test-Function Conventions: Examples

items.title: Conjugate phases norm a three-atom function
items.statement: On three atoms each of mass 1/3 let g=(1,omega,omega^2), omega=(-1+i sqrt(3))/2. Then ||g||1=1. The bilinear test s=(1,conjugate(omega),conjugate(omega)^2) has ||s||infinity=1 and integral gs=1. For real tests with ||s||infinity<=1 the largest modulus is 2/3, strictly smaller. Omitting conjugation and taking s=g gives integral g^2=0.
items.strategy: Compute omega^3=1 and 1+omega+omega^2=0 directly. A real triple in [-1,1]^3 is a convex combination of the eight sign vertices. The modulus of its image is bounded by the largest vertex modulus; equal-sign vertices give zero and all other vertices give 2/3. This proves the exact supremum, not just failure of one real test.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis
references.locator: §10.2 Corollary 10.5 supplies the phase test; the three-atom calculation is an original example.

items.title: Two-step functions expose the L2 conjugation convention
items.statement: Assume countable choice. On R with Lebesgue measure let f=1_[0,1)+i 1_[1,2) and g=i 1_[0,1)+1_[1,2). Then <f,g>=0 but integral fg=2i; ||f||2=||g||2=sqrt(2). Also <if,f>=2i while <f,if>=-2i. Thus the bilinear expression cannot be substituted for the inner product.
items.strategy: Integrate on the two disjoint unit intervals and conjugate the second coefficients explicitly. Display the two sums and the scalar-linearity check.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis

items.title: Mollification of a complex two-step function
items.statement: Assume countable choice. Let rho be a real nonnegative smooth unit-mass function supported in [-1,1], rho_epsilon(x)=epsilon^(-1)rho(x/epsilon), and f=1_[0,1]+i 1_[1,2]. Then (rho_epsilon*f)(x)=integral_{x-1}^x rho_epsilon(t)dt+i integral_{x-2}^{x-1}rho_epsilon(t)dt. It is smooth, supported in [-epsilon,2+epsilon], and converges to f in each finite Lp. For 0<epsilon<1/4, an explicit bound is ||rho_epsilon*f-f||p <= 2(6epsilon)^(1/p). Its error remains at least 1/2 in essential-supremum norm, because every continuous approximant to the jump at 0 has that lower bound.
items.strategy: Compute the two interval convolutions by t=x-y. Off epsilon-neighborhoods of 0,1,2 the convolution equals f; the error modulus is at most 2 on those neighborhoods, whose union has length at most 6epsilon. For the infinity warning use continuity at 0 and positive-measure one-sided intervals to show that errors strictly below 1/2 would force incompatible limits. This makes the finite-p restriction concrete.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis
